name: Marco Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or parties. What you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me your public view and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I teach history at St Aidan's, a Catholic boys' secondary on the hill above the market. I get in at seven, say morning prayer with my tutor group, then teach five periods, mostly Year 10 and 11 exam groups. After school three days a week I coach the under-14s football team on the back pitch.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the stories, honestly. When I tell the Year 9s about the trenches and the room goes quiet, that's the job. What wears me out is the paperwork from the trust: lesson plans in their template, data drops, behaviour logs on three different systems.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any AI tools in your work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: No, never. A couple of the younger staff use it to write reports, and the head keeps sending emails about 'trying it out'. I write my own reports by hand first, then type them, because a parent deserves to know I actually thought about their boy.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Fine. I'm on decent pay after taking on the history coursework lead, and I bought a one-bed flat on Mill Street two years ago with help from my parents. I've got around eight months of money put by on top of that. I'm single, I go to Mass on Sundays with my family, and my mum still feeds me twice a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, politely. In the staffroom I'd say teaching is a human job and always was. I don't really post online, but I'd say it at my dad's dinner table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means nothing changes for me, and that suits me. The trust might push some reports through a computer, and I'd probably still write mine myself. My job, my flat and my savings are steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am: teach, coach, go for head of history in a few years. I'd keep putting £400 a month into savings and pay a bit extra off the flat. If the head insisted on AI reports, I'd do the minimum and keep my own notes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, really. It would feel like the world came to its senses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the head insisted on AI reports, would you push back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to keep writing my own, and I'd explain why. If the answer was no, I'd do what I'm told, because I'm not a troublemaker. But I'd still read every one before it went home, line by line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that worries you in this world, even without AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Class sizes creep up every year, and the old building leaks. Mostly I worry about the boys, phones and gambling apps, not my own job. My own life is in good order, thank God.

say: I'd say **teaching is human** and always was, and that the hype missed the point.
I'd say it quietly at **family dinner** and in the staffroom, not online.
think: Nothing changes for me, and that **suits me** fine.
My job, my flat and my **savings are steady**, whatever the trust does with reports.
do: Keep teaching history and coaching, aiming for **head of history**.
Save **£400 a month** and overpay the flat a little.
Write **reports by hand** and read any AI version line by line.
feel: **Calm** and content, as if the world came to its senses.
S0.quote: Mostly I worry about the boys, phones and gambling apps, not my own job.
fieldNote: Marco never uses AI and sees **report writing** as a matter of respect for parents.
He'd **comply** if pushed but quietly keep his own standards.
His worries are about the **boys' phones**, not his own income.

steps.text: Keep teaching history and coaching the under-14s football team
Save £400 a month and overpay the Mill Street flat

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a teacher's job is to know the boys, and no program can do that. In the staffroom I'd back the union if the trust started cutting posts. Online, nothing, I'd leave that to others.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the trust would use it as an excuse. They'd say the AI writes the lesson plans and marks the essays, so a history teacher can take two more classes. I'd be fine for a while, but I'd be the one dragging my feet, and that gets noticed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join the union's working group on AI and turn up to every meeting. I'd learn the bare minimum of whatever system the trust buys, probably on a training day, because I'd have no choice. And I'd keep saving, maybe up to £500 a month, so I'm never forced to take a bad deal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. A bit resentful, if I'm honest, like being told to change how you pray.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn the bare minimum. What would that look like in the classroom?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd let the AI mark the multiple-choice quizzes, since those are just ticks. Essays I'd mark myself, with a red pen, because the comments are where I teach the boys to argue. If the head wanted the AI to do essays, I'd want that in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our teaching assistants, mostly. They do a lot of the photocopying, cover and paperwork, and the trust would see that as a saving. My friend Joe has been a teaching assistant at St Aidan's for fifteen years, and I don't know what he'd do.

say: I'd say a teacher's job is to **know the boys**.
I'd **back the union** if the trust cut posts.
think: The trust would use AI as an **excuse** for bigger loads.
Being **slow to adopt** would get noticed and could count against me.
do: Join the union's **AI working group** and attend every meeting.
Learn the **bare minimum** of the trust's system on training days.
feel: **Uneasy** and a bit resentful at being told to change.
S1.quote: Essays I'd mark myself, with a red pen, because the comments are where I teach the boys to argue.
fieldNote: He'd accept AI for **simple ticking** but guards essay marking as real teaching.
His main fear is for **teaching assistants**, like his friend Joe.
He senses resistance could **count against him**, a new pressure.

steps.text: Join the union's AI working group at St Aidan's
Learn the trust's marking system only for multiple-choice quizzes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say schools are about raising young men, not downloading facts. I'd say it at Mass, at the club, to anyone who asked. I'd want the bishops and the governors to say it loudly too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it frightens me more than I'd admit. If a machine can teach the causes of the First World War better than me by 2028, what's left is discipline, sport and pastoral care. A Catholic school might keep teachers longer because parents want people, but I'd expect fewer of us and lower pay within a couple of years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first months I'd talk to the head about moving more into pastoral work, maybe head of Year 8, because that's people work. I'd do a coaching qualification, the next football badge, so I've got something with my hands and my voice. I'd stop spending on anything big, keep the eight months in cash, and keep paying the flat down hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd be lying awake a bit. I've never used these tools, so I'd feel two steps behind the twenty-two-year-olds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said robots for hands-on work come around 2031. Does that matter for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It matters for the football, I suppose, and for standing in a corridor at break. Nobody's sending a robot to break up a fight on the back pitch in 2029, but history teaching is talk and essays. So for the lessons it's the 2028 date, not the later one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anyone in your family help you through it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad has a carpet shop, and he's always said there's a job there. I'd hate to take it, but I'd rather lay carpets with my dad than sit at home. Family is what you lean on, not the government.

say: I'd say schools are about **raising young men**.
I'd want the **bishops and governors** to say so loudly.
think: What's left of my job would be **discipline, sport** and pastoral care.
I'd expect **fewer teachers** and lower pay within a couple of years.
do: Ask the head about moving to **head of Year 8**.
Keep **eight months** in cash and pay the flat down hard.
feel: Feels **two steps behind** younger staff who already use AI.
S2.quote: Nobody's sending a robot to break up a fight on the back pitch in 2029, but history teaching is talk and essays.
fieldNote: He sees his job split: **history lessons** fall at the AGI date, coaching and pastoral work later.
He'd lean on **family**, not the state, with his dad's carpet shop as a fallback.
Never using AI leaves him feeling **behind**, which feeds the anxiety.

steps.text: Ask the head about becoming head of Year 8
Take the next football coaching badge
Keep eight months in cash and overpay the flat
Keep his dad's carpet shop as a fallback job

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same message, but louder: we have five years, so let's protect what matters. I'd push the governors to promise the boys always have a human form tutor. I'd stand for the staff seat on the governing body.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, five years doesn't make me feel much safer, because I know I'd spend the first two hoping it isn't true. That's my nature. I'd be 32 when it lands, which is young enough to change, but I'd be changing late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stand for staff governor this year, so I'm in the room when decisions get made. I'd do my football badges over two summers and ask to move into pastoral leadership by year three. I'd probably also make myself try the AI tools for a term, because I can't fight what I don't understand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but more steady than with two years. Like watching weather roll in over the hill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd make yourself try the tools. That's new from you.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, and I don't like it. But my grandad always said know your enemy, and he was a stubborn man too. I'd try AI on lesson planning first, not on anything with the boys' names.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut back, if anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, I don't spend much. Maybe I'd skip the new car and keep the old Corolla running. I'd want the flat paid off before 2031 if I could.

say: I'd say we have **five years** to protect what matters.
I'd push for every boy to keep a **human form tutor**.
think: I'd waste **two years hoping** it isn't true, because that's my nature.
At 32 I'd be **changing late**, even if young enough.
do: Earn **football badges** and move into pastoral leadership by year three.
Try **AI for lesson planning** for one term.
feel: **Anxious** but steadier, like weather rolling in over the hill.
S3.quote: My grandad always said know your enemy, and he was a stubborn man too. I'd try AI on lesson planning first, not on anything with the boys' names.
fieldNote: Five years only slightly eases him; he expects his own **delay** to waste time.
For the first time he'd **try AI**, framed as knowing the enemy.
He wants a **voice** through the governing body rather than protest.

steps.text: Stand for the staff seat on the governing body
Try AI tools for lesson planning for one term
Earn football badges and move into pastoral leadership
Skip a new car and keep the old Corolla

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is time to do it properly, and I'd want the church schools to lead. I'd say parents should get a say in how much screen teaching their boys get. That's a message people at Mass would agree with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years is enough that I'd probably be fine. By 2036 I'd hope to be head of history or head of year, and the people side of that lasts. I'd still be uneasy, because I'd see young teachers coming in who might never get a full post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep teaching and coaching and go for head of history when it comes up. I'd pay the flat off by about 2033, then save hard. I'd probably also think about marrying and settling sooner, because I'd want a family home bought before the world gets strange.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I could live with it. Ten years is a long time in a school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned marriage. Is that a real plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a girl from church, Clare, and we've been seeing each other for a few months. I wouldn't rush it because of computers. But knowing the world changes in ten years, I'd want my roots down by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if it went badly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The tech firms first, and governments who let them run ahead. Also schools that bought the shiny thing instead of hiring people. Not the teachers, they'd just be doing what they're told.

say: I'd say ten years is time to **do it properly**.
I'd want **parents** to have a **say** in screen teaching.
think: I'd probably be fine, with **head of history** or head of year by 2036.
I'd be uneasy for **young teachers** who may never get a post.
do: Go for **head of history** when the post opens.
Pay off the **flat by 2033**, then save hard.
Settle down with **Clare** sooner and buy a family home.
feel: **Uneasy** but able to live with it.
S4.quote: Knowing the world changes in ten years, I'd want my roots down by then.
fieldNote: Ten years lets him keep his **old plan** with small adjustments.
He blames **tech firms** and governments, never teachers.
His new urgency is about **marriage and a home**, not career change.

steps.text: Apply for head of history when the post opens
Pay off the Mill Street flat by 2033
Plan marriage and a family home with Clare sooner

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, without question. Two years is no time for a man like me who's slow with this stuff. What would help is a rule that every child has a real teacher as their form tutor, and proper training paid for by the trust, not something squeezed into a Friday afternoon.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what the boys think. They're the ones who'll grow up with it. I teach history because the past tells you who you are, and I'd hate a generation that only knows what a machine told them.

headlineQuote: I teach history because the past tells you who you are, and I'd hate a generation that only knows what a machine told them.
portrait: Marco is a **27-year-old history teacher** and football coach at St Aidan's, a Catholic boys' school.
He has never used AI, owns a **one-bed flat** and has eight months saved.
He's calm if AI stalls and **uneasy** about trust pressure in slower change.
Fast AGI makes him **anxious**; he'd move to pastoral work and lean on family.
With more time he'd **try AI**, seek a governor seat and settle down.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years is no time for someone slow with **technology**.
whatWouldHelp: A rule that every child has a **human form tutor**.
Proper **paid training** from the trust, not a rushed Friday afternoon.
